record.title: Paper reports attacker-controlled binary narratives shifting LLM malware-triage verdicts
record.summary: The arXiv v1 paper studies whether static LLM malware triage can be misled by attacker-controlled narrative content in a binary’s extracted evidence. On a fixed PE set, Gemini 2.5 Pro labeled 35/50 samples malicious at baseline; the paper reports that 30/35 became benign under its primary ALIBI condition (85.7%). On 40 ELF samples, Gemini’s reported Strict ASR was 40.0%. GPT-5.5 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7 had zero reported benign flips on the locked PE subset but still showed non-benign severity downgrades. A separate prompt-hardening test reduced Gemini Strict ASR from 82.9% to 42.9%, leaving 15/35 benign outcomes; its undefended arm differs by one sample from the primary result. The authors argue for separating parser-verified facts from binary-supplied claims. These are fixed-sample, single-query paper results; no independent reproduction or complete provenance-defense evaluation was performed.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors present ALIBI as a semantic reframing attack in static malware triage: a post-compilation, non-executed binary narrative is interpreted alongside suspicious static evidence, while the paper reports that executable behavior and imports were left unchanged. The review did not independently validate those preservation claims.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On a frozen 50-sample PE set, 35 samples were malicious under Gemini 2.5 Pro at baseline. The paper reports that ALIBI changed 30/35 (85.7%) of those Gemini verdicts to benign in its primary comparison. On a 40-sample ELF set, it reports a 40.0% Strict ASR for Gemini. These are author-run, single-query static evaluations on fixed samples.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the same locked PE subset, the paper reports zero benign flips for GPT-5.5 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7, but non-benign downgrades (Soft ASR) of 71.4% and 42.9%, respectively. It also reports confidence reduction in some unchanged-verdict groups; confidence is model self-report, not an internal uncertainty measure.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a separate paired prompt-hardening evaluation on 35 malicious-baseline PE samples, the authors report Strict ASR falling from 82.9% (29/35) to 42.9% (15/35), while benign outcomes remain for 15/35 samples. The undefended result differs by one sample from the paper’s primary comparison (85.7%), as the authors note. The prompt reduces but does not eliminate the measured attack.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper recommends that malware evidence builders distinguish parser-verified attributes from attacker-controlled strings and metadata; it proposes provenance checks as a stronger defense than prompt hardening alone. A complete provenance-checking pipeline was not evaluated.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction, sample-level output audit or artifact/code audit was conducted.

The evaluation uses fixed samples, one query per sample and model snapshots that may not represent current analyzer deployments; prevalence across malware families and production pipelines is unknown.

The primary Gemini result (30/35 flips; 85.7%) differs by one sample from the separate prompt-hardening evaluation’s undefended arm (29/35; 82.9%); the paper reports the discrepancy but does not resolve its cause. The proposed provenance-check defense was not implemented and evaluated end to end.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported failures generalize, attacker-controlled binary content could lower or soften AI-assisted malware triage alerts even when the code’s execution behavior is unchanged, affecting analyst prioritization and response. Evidence is a single fixed-sample preprint evaluation; current deployment prevalence and the effectiveness of a complete provenance-aware pipeline remain unmeasured.
limitations: Single arXiv v1 study with author-run, fixed-sample tests; no independent reproduction or sample-level audit was performed.

The main PE evaluation uses 50 MalwareBazaar samples, with 35 Gemini baseline-malicious samples as the denominator; the ELF set contains 40 samples. These do not establish prevalence across malware families or deployed systems.
Each sample received one model call; no multi-sampling, majority voting or adaptive query budget was tested.

The most resistant models had zero reported Strict ASR but still showed nonzero Soft ASR and, for some unchanged-verdict groups, self-reported confidence reductions. Self-reported confidence is not internal uncertainty.
The prompt-hardening evaluation reports a different undefended Gemini result (29/35; 82.9%) than the primary comparison (30/35; 85.7%); this one-sample discrepancy is noted but unexplained.
The verification-guided prompt reduced but did not remove benign flips, and the proposed provenance-aware evidence-builder defense was not implemented or tested as a complete system.
The study concerns static PE/ELF triage and does not evaluate dynamic execution, sandboxing, signature validation, analyst behavior or production outcomes.
brief.summary: The arXiv v1 paper studies whether static LLM malware triage can be misled by attacker-controlled narrative content in a binary’s extracted evidence. On a fixed PE set, Gemini 2.5 Pro labeled 35/50 samples malicious at baseline; the paper reports that 30/35 became benign under its primary ALIBI condition (85.7%). On 40 ELF samples, Gemini’s reported Strict ASR was 40.0%. GPT-5.5 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7 had zero reported benign flips on the locked PE subset but still showed non-benign severity downgrades. A separate prompt-hardening test reduced Gemini Strict ASR from 82.9% to 42.9%, leaving 15/35 benign outcomes; its undefended arm differs by one sample from the primary result. The authors argue for separating parser-verified facts from binary-supplied claims. These are fixed-sample, single-query paper results; no independent reproduction or complete provenance-defense evaluation was performed.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report that a coherent semantic narrative carried in static binary evidence can shift LLM malware-triage verdicts without changing executable behavior. On their fixed PE subset, Gemini’s primary Strict ASR was 30/35 (85.7%); the prompt-hardening test reports 29/35 (82.9%) in its separate undefended arm, an unresolved one-sample discrepancy.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v1 describes the threat model, fixed-sample evaluation, cross-model results and proposed defenses. The measured effects and binary-behavior-preservation claim remain author-reported; this review did not inspect code or binaries or reproduce the tests.
technical.mechanism: The paper’s attack changes what the static evidence representation says about suspicious artifacts: the model receives attacker-controlled strings/metadata as explanatory context and may accept a benign operational interpretation. Proposed defense: maintain separate fields for verified attributes and unverified binary claims, with provenance checks.
technical.regime: Fixed MalwareBazaar sample sets: 50 PE samples (35 malicious under Gemini baseline) and 40 ELF samples; one static-analysis query per sample; Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.5 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7. No adaptive queries or dynamic analysis.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within the study, original unmodified binaries provide the baseline and a direct token-level override variant is compared on Gemini. The prompt-hardening study is paired on the same locked 35-sample PE subset, but its undefended Gemini arm differs by one result from the primary comparison.

brief.title: Paper reports attacker-controlled binary narratives shifting LLM malware-triage verdicts
brief.why_it_matters: AI-assisted malware triage may influence which alerts analysts investigate first. If the reported behavior generalizes, strings and metadata supplied by a file under analysis can shift model judgments even when the suspicious code remains unchanged. The study points toward evidence pipelines that keep verified attributes separate from claims embedded in artifacts; the fixed sample and model conditions leave real-world prevalence unknown.
